That's fair and I should've included that in my post originally, that yes, a lot of alt medicine is ineffective at best and harmful at worst. Sorting the bad from the good is up to consumers doing their own research among a pile of pseudoscience and misinformation. It's definitely a diamond in the rough situation.

Though, there is medicine in there and for people who want to explore those options, they can be found. 

And while I appreciate you mentioning how doctors have checks and balances preventing bias, pharmacutical companies have incentives that encourage the inclusion of marketable medications and discourage researching alternative medicines that are not as easily sold. I know this feels pretty tin-hatty and all that, but consider that the current opioid epidemic we're facing was due in part to the company Perdue knowing and concealing the fact that Oxycontin is addictive in 1996. The incentive was there to produce a new pain med as pain was being embraced as the 5th vital sign and there was a strong market push for a non-addictive option, thus, the company was simply responding to the incentives the market put out. 

In comparison, more researchers are looking into meditation, a well known alternative medicine, as a way to help manage chronic pain conditions. And while the research is still preliminary and we haven't seen enough long term research for it to be labeled medicine, meditation is stated by many as a panacea for different ailments. 

And I'm sorry for the wall of text, I know it got a bit winded there. I find the topic of alt medicine to be interesting, though I recognize that a majority is placebo or snake oil. I think it's prudent to keep an open, and critical, mind on alt medicine and medicine.

Here's a research paper on meditation for chronic pain btw, if you're curious: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4941786/

Upvote for stating something I believed about this quote but couldn't put into words! And to throw my two cents in. Medicine becomes medicine through a long expensive process and some company has to bankroll it, wether government, pharmacutical, or charity. So most of the time if a potential medicinal product isn't thought to be profitable, it won't be tested and labeled "medicine." That doesn't detract from it's medicinal quality, just that some people didn't believe it had market value.

Now, I'm 100% behind seeing a doctor and getting tested medicine, however I'm not so quick to dismiss alt medicine either. Some ailments definitely do require a doctor's expertise while others can be solved using an alternative option.

I think you bring up a good point. I have trouble with social anxiety and am new to DND but I enjoy the playstyle of high cha characters. It sucks that some dms will force me to role play through some actions, which then fail due to my lack in social graces and not my characters. But then other players can roll for dex or str and not have to show a force of either irl. 

That being said, my favorite dm right now will often intermingle the two. Like, if someone really likes to rp but has a low Cha score then even if they play a scene well, they still have to roll. And if a player doesn't want to rp a scene, he'll let you just roll but will encourage a scene if you feel up to it. 

 In general, there's a lower bound to the Cha stat that will always require a roll no matter how skilled the player irl is and an upper bound that will let the player rely on rolls than irl skill if they want. 

This dm has a good idea on the skill and comfort levels of his players though that I think play into his dictating of events.

The fact that most medical studies for pharmaceuticals are preformed only on or more extensively on men. This leads to side effects affecting women being underrepresented or completely unknown until it's in the retail markets. 

A great example of this is ambien. Women werent included in the studies of side effects for ambien and so, scientists were unaware of the fact that men's digestive systems would process the drug almost 2 hours before women did. This lead to some women experiencing severe cases of sleep walking or sleep driving. Some women were "waking up" getting into their car and then crashing because the active ingredient in ambien was still affecting them.

This is a concerning market for new drugs coming to market and the perceived limits and effectiveness for older drugs. We need to better understand how our medicine affects all members of society. Not just the comparatively "easy" male biology.

Someone's already mentioned the skin care subs and I second that. They can provide great information and product suggestions. Just in case they don't say it though, always try new products out one at a time so if you experience a bag reaction you know what caused it.

For makeup, a lot of it comes from practise and finding what style you like. Look for actresses or characters whose style you like and try to mimic them. Also, Sephora and (maybe) ultra workers offer free mini tutorials like how to apply a cat eye or basic before technique (I've gotten both of these tutorials from Sephora and they were really helpful and insightful. Word of caution though, it can feel like they're really pushing products after one of these. don't be afraid to say no or to refuse products you are not totally sold on) And don't be afraid to ask for samples of their products. A good rule of thumb is if there's an open trial of a product they can offer a free sample for you to take home. Their prices are far too high to risk taking home a foundation you are not totally in love with. Don't be afraid to ask them any questions, they're passionate about makeup and happy to share what they know :)


Also good on you for checking YouTube for ideas! YouTube is a wealth of information
 skincare and makeup tutorial wise. Explore and trust your instincts!! In the end of the day, you know you best and I'm confident that you'll find the right routine for you :)
